title: How do you check who logged into an EC2 instance and inspect its logs without CloudWatch (`/var/log/auth.log` or `secure`, `last`, console output)?
shortTitle: Checking Logins and Inspecting Logs on EC2 Without CloudWatch
topicTitle: How do you check who logged into an EC2 instance and inspect its logs without Cl

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Even without CloudWatch, a Linux EC2 instance records authentication and system activity locally. Interactive and SSH logins are written to the authentication log — `/var/log/auth.log` on Debian and Ubuntu, `/var/log/secure` on Amazon Linux and Red Hat. The `last` and `lastb` commands read the binary login records (`wtmp` and `btmp`) to show successful and failed logins, `who` shows current sessions, and application and system logs live under `/var/log` or are queried through `journalctl`. The EC2 console's system log and screenshot features let you inspect a box that you cannot even SSH into.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** CloudWatch is like National Bank of India's central security control room that collects every branch's footage in one place. But even without that central room, each branch still keeps its own visitor book at the door recording who entered and when, a separate book of rejected visitors, and its own CCTV tapes in a cupboard. So you walk to that branch and read its door register (`auth.log` or `secure`), its entry list (`last`), its rejection list (`lastb`), and its tapes (the other logs). And if the branch door is jammed shut, head office can still peek at a snapshot of the lobby (EC2 console system log and screenshot).

**One line to remember:** Logins live in the auth log and in `last`/`lastb`, current sessions in `who`, everything else under `/var/log` and `journalctl`, and the EC2 console system log works even when SSH does not.

sections.s2_technical:
The authentication log is the first place to look for who logged in. On Ubuntu and Debian it is `/var/log/auth.log`; on Amazon Linux and Red Hat it is `/var/log/secure`. Every SSH login, every `sudo` command, and every failed password attempt is recorded there with a timestamp and source IP.

```bash
# Who authenticated, and failed attempts, with source IPs
sudo grep "Accepted"  /var/log/secure      # successful SSH logins (Amazon Linux)
sudo grep "Failed"    /var/log/secure      # failed attempts — possible attack
sudo grep "sudo"      /var/log/secure      # privilege escalations
```

The `last` command reads the binary `wtmp` file and prints a history of successful logins and logouts, including the user, the source IP, and the session duration. The `lastb` command reads `btmp` and prints failed login attempts, which is how you spot a brute-force attempt. The `who` command shows who is logged in right now, and `w` shows what each active user is doing.

```bash
last -a                    # login history with hostnames/IPs
sudo lastb -a              # failed login attempts (brute force signal)
who                        # currently logged-in sessions
w                          # active sessions + current activity
```

Application and service logs live under `/var/log` — for example `/var/log/messages` or `/var/log/syslog` for general system events, and the application's own files such as `/var/log/settlement-service/app.log`. On systemd-based systems the modern way is `journalctl`, which queries the journal by service, time range, and priority.

```bash
journalctl -u settlement-service --since "1 hour ago"   # one service's recent logs
journalctl -p err -b                                     # errors since last boot
tail -f /var/log/settlement-service/app.log              # follow live app output
```

Finally, when you cannot SSH in at all, the EC2 console provides the instance system log (the serial console boot output) and an instance screenshot, retrievable through the console or the CLI. These come from the hypervisor, not from inside the instance, so they work even when the box is unreachable over the network.

```bash
aws ec2 get-console-output --instance-id i-0abc --output text   # boot/kernel log
```

A senior nuance: local logs are lost if the instance is terminated, and an attacker with root can tamper with them. That is exactly why in production we still ship logs off the box — to CloudWatch Logs or an ELK stack — so there is a tamper-resistant, durable copy. But for live incident response and for forensics on a box without CloudWatch, these local tools are indispensable, and for a bank the auth log and `lastb` output are often the first evidence in a security investigation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Something changed on the settlement server and the team suspects an unauthorized login, but CloudWatch was never configured on this legacy box. This is exactly what the local auth log and `last`/`lastb` solve: they record every successful and failed login with source IP and time, directly on the instance.

Problem 2 — The team must also see what the application did around that time and whether there were errors. This is exactly what the `/var/log` application log and `journalctl` provide.

We will build a `LoginAuditor` that parses auth-log lines into login events and flags suspicious failed-attempt bursts, plus a `LogInspector` that filters application log lines by level and time. Classes: `LoginEvent`, `LoginAuditor`, `LogInspector`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four authentication-log lines (one successful login, three failed attempts from the same external IP) and three application-log lines.

Step 1 — The `LoginAuditor` parses each auth line. The first contains "Accepted," so it becomes a successful `LoginEvent` for `ec2-user` from the internal IP 10.0.1.5. The next three contain "Failed," so they become failed events from the external IP 203.0.113.9.

Step 2 — The auditor prints each event, giving an immediate human-readable record of who got in and who was rejected, with source IPs — exactly what `last` and `lastb` would show on the real box.

Step 3 — The auditor counts failed attempts per source IP. The external IP has three failures, at or above the threshold, so it is flagged as a suspected brute-force source. On the real instance this corresponds to reading `/var/log/secure` and `lastb` for repeated failures from one address.

Step 4 — The `LogInspector` filters the application log for SEVERE lines, surfacing the failure to reach NPCI. This mirrors using `journalctl -p err` or grepping the app log to find errors around the incident time.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] LOGIN OK ec2-user from 10.0.1.5
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] LOGIN FAIL admin from 203.0.113.9
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] LOGIN FAIL root from 203.0.113.9
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] LOGIN FAIL oracle from 203.0.113.9
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Brute-force suspected from: [203.0.113.9]
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] SEVERE lines: [SEVERE settlement failed to reach NPCI]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  EC2 instance (no CloudWatch)
    │
    ├─ /var/log/secure (auth.log) ──→ grep Accepted/Failed/sudo
    ├─ wtmp/btmp ───────────────────→ last / lastb (login history, failures)
    ├─ who / w ─────────────────────→ current sessions
    ├─ /var/log/* , journalctl ─────→ app + system logs by level/time
    └─ (SSH dead?) hypervisor ──────→ aws ec2 get-console-output / screenshot
         │
         ▼
  LoginAuditor.parse → events → bruteForceSources → flag 203.0.113.9
  LogInspector.byLevel("SEVERE") → surface the error
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Even without CloudWatch, a Linux EC2 instance keeps a full record of activity locally, and knowing where to look is a core operations and incident-response skill. The first place I go to find who logged in is the authentication log — on Ubuntu and Debian it is slash var slash log slash auth dot log, and on Amazon Linux and Red Hat it is slash var slash log slash secure. Every SSH login, every sudo command, and every failed password attempt is recorded there with a timestamp and a source IP, so grepping for Accepted shows me successful logins, grepping for Failed shows me attacks, and grepping for sudo shows privilege escalations.

Alongside the text log there are the binary login records. The last command reads wtmp and prints the history of successful logins and logouts with user, source IP, and session length, while lastb reads btmp and prints failed attempts, which is exactly how I spot a brute-force attack — many failures from one address in a short window. For live state, who shows who is logged in right now and w shows what each active user is doing. For application and system behaviour I read the files under slash var slash log, and on modern systemd boxes I use journalctl to query by service, time range, and priority, so I can pull one service's errors in the last hour.

There is one more tool that matters when the box is so broken I cannot even SSH in: the EC2 console system log and instance screenshot. Those come from the hypervisor, not from inside the instance, so they work even when the instance is unreachable over the network, and they often show me a kernel panic or a full disk that explains why SSH is dead.

At National Bank of India we had a legacy settlement server without CloudWatch, and when we suspected an unauthorized login I read slash var slash log slash secure and ran lastb, which immediately showed a burst of failed attempts from one external IP — a clear brute-force signature — while last confirmed the only successful login was our own engineer from the internal network. The senior point I always add is that local logs are lost if the instance is terminated and a root attacker can tamper with them, so in production we still ship logs off the box to CloudWatch or an ELK stack for a durable, tamper-resistant copy. But for forensics on a box that never had CloudWatch, these local tools are exactly what you reach for first.
